related_resources.reason: Describes contemporary subak groups, temple networks and historical roots; living practices do not prove identical medieval institutions.
Argues that coordinated planting and irrigation can balance water and pest dynamics; model is about a functioning system, not direct historical proof of its medieval structure.
Summarizes dated Old Balinese inscriptions, kasuwakan and water specialists and granted irrigation rights; inscriptions document named rights, not a complete millennium of unchanged practice.
Treats rulers, regional lords, water temples and redistribution as intertwined rather than separate state and farmers-only spheres.
Challenges a wholly bottom-up account of water management: royal and colonial authorities played significant roles, based on historical archives and fieldwork.
Supplementary article for orientation only; no historical claim relies on this source.
